source_text: Et haec quidem diuinae patientiae species, quasi de longinquo, fors ut de supernis aestimetur. quid illa autem, quae inter homines palam in terris quodammodo manu adprehensa est? nasci se deus in utero patitur matris [expectat] et natus adolescere sustinet et adultus non gestit agnosci, sed contumeliosus insuper sibi est et a seruo suo tinguitur et temptatoris congressus solis uerbis repellit. cum de deo fit magister docens hominem euadere mortem, ob salutem scilicet ueniam offensae patientiae eruditum, (non contendit, non reclamauit nec quisquam in plateis uocem eius audiuit; arundinem quassatam non fregit, linum fumigans non restinxit.) nec enim mentitus fuerat propheta, immo ipsius dei contestatio, spiritum suum in filio cum tota patientia collocantis. nullum uolentem sibi adhaerere non suscepit, nullius mensam tectumue despexit; [atquin ipse lauandis discipulorum pedibus ministrauit] non peccatores, non publicanos aspernatus est, non illi saltim ciuitati, quae eum recipere noluerat, iratus est, cum etiam discipuli tam contumelioso oppido caelestes ignes repraesentari uoluissent; ingratos curauit, insidiatoribus cessit. parum hoc, si non etiam proditorem suum secum habuit nec constanter denotauit. cum uero traditur, cum adducitur ut pecus ad uictimam, — sic enim non magis aperit os quam agnus sub tondentis potestate — ille, cui legiones angelorum, si uoluisset, uno dicto de caelis adfuissent, ne unius quidem discentis gladium ultorem probauit. patientia domini in Malcho uulnerata est. itaque et gladii opera maledixit in posterum et sanitatis restitutione ei, quem non ipse uexauerat, satisfecit per patientiam, misericordiae matrem. taceo, quod figitur; in hoc enim uenerat. numquid tamen subiendae morti etiam contumeliis opus fuerat? sed saginari uoluptate patientiae discessurus uolebat: despuitur, uerberatur, deridetur, foedis uestitur, foedioribus coronatur. mira aequanimitatis fides: qui in hominis figura proposuerat latere, nihil de impatientia hominis imitatus est. hinc uel maxime, Pharisaei, dominum agnoscere debuistis; patientiam huiusmodi nemo hominum perpetraret. talia tantaque documenta, quorum magnitudo penes nationes quidem detrectatio fidei est, penes nos uero ratio et structio, satis aperte non sermonibus modo in praecipiendo sed etiam passionibus domini (in) sustinendo probant his, quibus credere datum est, patientiam dei esse naturam, effectum et praestantiam ingenitae cuiusdam proprietatis.
thought_title: Christ's patience on earth as proof of divine nature
orientation: Tertullian has just described God's patience from afar in his forbearance toward the world; now he turns to the patience God displayed openly among human beings in the person of Christ.
pass_a_gloss: And this kind of divine patience is, as it were, from far off, perhaps so that it may be judged from the heights. But what about that patience which was openly grasped by hand, so to speak, among human beings on earth? God allows himself to be born in the womb of a mother, and once born he endures growing up, and once grown he does not desire to be recognized, but moreover he is insulting to himself, and he is baptized by his own servant, and he repels the attacks of the tempter with words alone. When from being God he becomes a teacher, teaching a human being to escape death, namely for salvation, instructed in the pardon of offense by patience, he does not contend, he did not cry out, nor did anyone hear his voice in the streets; a bruised reed he did not break, and smoking flax he did not extinguish. For the prophet had not lied, or rather the testimony of God himself, placing his own spirit in his son with all patience. He did not fail to receive anyone willing to cling to him, he despised no one's table or roof; indeed he himself ministered in washing the feet of the disciples; he did not spurn sinners, nor tax collectors, he was not angry even with that city which had refused to receive him, even when his disciples wanted heavenly fires to be brought down upon so insulting a town; he healed the ungrateful, he yielded to those plotting against him. This is too little, if he did not also have his betrayer with him and did not firmly mark him out. But when he is handed over, when he is led like a sheep to the slaughter—for thus he no more opens his mouth than a lamb under the power of its shearer—he, to whom legions of angels, if he had wished, would have come from heaven at one word, did not approve even the avenging sword of one disciple. The patience of the Lord was wounded in Malchus. And so he both cursed the work of the sword for the future and by the restoration of health to him whom he himself had not harmed, he made satisfaction through patience, the mother of mercy. I pass over that he is nailed to the cross; for he had come for this. But was there need of insults also for undergoing death? But he who was about to depart wished to be fattened with the pleasure of patience: he is spat upon, he is scourged, he is mocked, he is clothed in foul things, he is crowned with fouler things. Wonderful is the faith of his equanimity: he who had resolved to lie hidden in the figure of a human being imitated nothing of human impatience. From this especially, Pharisees, you ought to have recognized the Lord; no human being would accomplish patience of this kind. Such and so great proofs, whose greatness among the pagans is indeed a refusal of faith, but among us is reason and edification, prove clearly enough—not only by words in teaching but also by the sufferings of the Lord in enduring—to those to whom it has been given to believe, that patience is the nature of God, the effect and excellence of an inborn property.

choices.english: as it were, from far off
choices.why: Preserves the distancing metaphor Tertullian uses to contrast the earlier, remote view of divine patience with the close, tangible patience of Christ.
Keeps the tactile, concrete image of patience made physically present and observable among humans.

choices.english: moreover he is insulting to himself
choices.why: Renders the reflexive sense that Christ willingly accepted dishonor against himself, matching the source's compact expression.

choices.english: to be fattened with the pleasure of patience
choices.why: Preserves the striking metaphor of being nourished or filled by patience's delight, which is central to Tertullian's rhetoric.
rejected: to be fed with the pleasure of patience
to feast on the pleasure of patience

choices.why: Captures the active rejection of faith by pagans, not merely a passive lack of belief.
Renders the paired terms as the intellectual and constructive benefit these proofs have for believers.

pass_b_english: And this is the appearance of divine patience, to be judged as it were from far off, perhaps from the heavens. But what of that patience which was grasped by hand, openly, among human beings on earth? God allows himself to be born in a mother's womb, and once born he endures growing up, and once grown he does not rush to be recognized. Moreover he allows himself to be insulted: he is baptized by his own servant, and he repels the tempter's attacks with words alone. When he who is God becomes a teacher, teaching a human being to escape death—trained in patience, of course, for the sake of salvation and the pardon of offenses—he does not strive or cry out, nor does anyone hear his voice in the streets; a bruised reed he does not break, and smoking flax he does not quench (Isaiah 42:2-3). For the prophet had not lied—indeed it was the testimony of God himself, placing his Spirit in his Son with all patience. He refused no one who wished to cling to him; he despised no one's table or roof. He did not spurn sinners or tax collectors; indeed, he himself ministered in washing the disciples' feet. He was not even angry at the city that had refused to receive him, though his disciples wanted heavenly fires brought down on so insolent a town. He healed the ungrateful and yielded to those who plotted against him. This is little, if he did not also keep his own betrayer with him and did not firmly mark him out. And when he is handed over, when he is led away like a sheep to the slaughter—for he does not open his mouth any more than a lamb under the power of its shearer (Isaiah 53:7)—he who could have had legions of angels at his side from heaven with a single word, if he had wished, did not approve even one disciple's sword as an avenger. The Lord's patience was wounded in Malchus. And so he cursed the works of the sword for the future, and by restoring to health the one he himself had not harmed, he made satisfaction through patience, the mother of mercy. I say nothing of his being nailed to the cross; for this he had come. But was there any need for insults as well as undergoing death? He wished to be filled with the pleasure of patience as he was about to depart. He is spat upon, beaten, mocked, clothed in foul garments, crowned with fouler ones. What marvelous faith of equanimity: he who had resolved to hide in human form imitated nothing of human impatience. From this above all, Pharisees, you should have recognized the Lord; no human being would have accomplished patience of this kind. Such great and numerous proofs—whose greatness is a refusal of faith among the pagans, but among us is reason and edification—prove clearly, not only by words in commanding but also by the Lord's sufferings in enduring, to those to whom it has been given to believe, that patience is God's nature, the effect and excellence of a certain innate property.

problems.quote: He did not spurn sinners or tax collectors.
problems.why: The Latin includes a clause that Christ himself washed the disciples’ feet, which the English omits.
problems.fix: He did not spurn sinners or tax collectors, and he himself washed the disciples’ feet.
problems.ruling: Source 'atquin ipse lauandis discipulorum pedibus ministrauit' (he washed disciples' feet) is entirely omitted, losing meaning.

edits.old: He did not spurn sinners or tax collectors.
edits.new: He did not spurn sinners or tax collectors; indeed, he himself ministered in washing the disciples' feet.

fixed: Added the omitted clause about Christ washing the disciples' feet, matching the source '[atquin ipse lauandis discipulorum pedibus ministrauit]'.

problems.quote: He received no one who wished to cling to him
problems.source_quote: nullum uolentem sibi adhaerere non suscepit
problems.why: Double negative means he received ALL who wished to cling to him.
problems.fix: He refused no one who wished to cling to him
problems.ruling: source "nullum ... non suscepit" is a double negative, meaning he received everyone, not "no one"

edits.old: He received no one who wished to cling to him
edits.new: He refused no one who wished to cling to him

fixed: Negation fixed: 'nullum uolentem sibi adhaerere non suscepit' means he received all who wished to cling to him, so 'He refused no one who wished to cling to him' is correct.

problems.fix: he is stained by his own servant

edits.old: he is baptized by his own servant
edits.new: he is stained by his own servant

fixed: Changed 'baptized' to 'stained': source 'tinguitur' means 'is stained/colored', not baptism.

dismissed.quote: I say nothing of his being nailed to the cross; for this he had come.
dismissed.why: English adds a specific reference to the crucifixion that is not in the Latin source.
dismissed.note: 'Quod figitur' means his being fixed or nailed to the cross, so the English adds nothing.

polish.changed: Clarified that Christ allowed himself to be insulted and baptized, and rendered the metaphor of being filled with the pleasure of patience more naturally.

notes.why: Unclear whether this means Christ allowed himself to be insulted or was insulting.
notes.fix: Clarify: 'he allowed himself to be insulted.'

notes.why: Odd metaphor; 'fattened with pleasure' reads strangely in context of the Passion.
notes.fix: Consider 'he wished to be filled with the sweetness of patience.'
